entities.name: Yan Hui
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Yan Hui, known reverently as Yan Yuan or Master Yan, was a seminal Chinese philosopher and the preeminent disciple of Confucius, flourishing during the tumultuous Spring and Autumn period (771–476 BCE) in ancient China. Though his exact birth year is unrecorded, his death in 480 BCE places him firmly within the Classical Era, where his exemplary virtue, profound understanding of Confucian doctrine, and unwavering devotion made him the ultimate model for all subsequent Confucian scholars. He is celebrated as one of the Four Sages and Ten Wise Ones in Confucian temples, symbolizing the ideal student and inheritor of the Master's Way.

Yan Hui's life was characterized by an extraordinary dedication to learning and a profound personal humility. Despite living in abject poverty, often subsisting on a single bamboo bowl of rice and a gourd of water, he never allowed material hardship to deter his pursuit of wisdom, earning Confucius's highest praise for his contentment and unwavering joy in the Dao. He served as Confucius's primary companion during the Master's arduous travels across various states, absorbing and internalizing the core tenets of humaneness (ren) and ritual propriety (li) with unmatched insight. His early and unexpected death at the age of 41 deeply grieved Confucius, who lamented, 'Heaven is destroying me! Heaven is destroying me!'

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Yan Hui's role as the ideal Confucian disciple and his subsequent veneration profoundly shaped the development and popularization of Confucian ideals across East Asia for millennia, serving as an enduring moral exemplar.
